prize_parts.citation: for the invention and development of optical lattice clocks, which brought atomic frequency standards to the 10^-18 level and opened new tests of fundamental physics

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: B022 alone, credited to Katori and Ye. The round-1 exchange sharpened rather than weakened the case. Katori's magic-wavelength lattice is a genuine conceptual step, because it lets thousands of atoms be interrogated free of Doppler, recoil and first-order light shifts, and Ye's programme turned that concept into record systematic uncertainty, coherence times and many-body clock operation. The 10^-18 level has been reached and compared in several independent laboratories, so reproducibility is not in question. That is what separates it most clearly from the other candidates under discussion, where either the interpretation (B028) or the credit (B002, B037) is still contested. I also answer the chair's question directly: the case does not depend on the pending redefinition of the second, which is a metrological decision and not a scientific test. It rests on demonstrated capabilities, namely the relativistic redshift resolved over centimetre height differences, clock-comparison limits on drifts of constants, and constraints on certain dark-matter couplings. The citation should name the lattice clock explicitly so that it reads as a distinct step beyond the comb-based work honoured in 2005 and the single-ion control honoured in 2012.
statement.case_against: The thematic overlap with the 2005 and 2012 prizes is real, and Mehlig's view that the work is more technological than conceptual cannot be dismissed. My answer is that the lattice concept itself is new and the gain in precision is orders of magnitude, but a committee that wants to avoid a third prize in precision atomic physics could reasonably wait. Attribution between Katori's concept and Ye's accuracy and many-body work is not fully separable, and Lemonde, Derevianko, the Takamoto and Ludlow generation and the ion-clock groups lie outside the two names. Some of the fundamental-physics reach, for example dark-matter searches, is still more a bound than a discovery, as Danielsson and Eriksson note. Finally, I must concede that B028 has the broadest support, and if its interpretation proves stable it is the strongest rival.

responses.point: He prefers B028 and asks Lindroth and me whether the fundamental-physics reach of the lattice clock is already demonstrated or still prospective.
responses.response: I will answer as asked. Demonstrated: clock comparisons at the 10^-18 level between independent laboratories; the gravitational redshift resolved over about a centimetre; and limits on temporal variation of the fine-structure constant and electron-to-proton mass ratio that are competitive with other methods. Prospective: any positive detection of new physics, and the redefinition of the second. I agree with your point that the clock case is a precision-measurement result, and I would not call a dark-matter claim established. But a prize for a measurement capability that has already opened these tests fits the tradition of the physics prizes. I note also that you accept the clean attribution, and your own reservation about B028 is its young field and the unsettled pairing, which you list as the central uncertainty.

responses.point: She argues that B028 is secure as a discovery, since many groups confirmed the flat-band correlated phases and only the interpretation of the superconductivity is open.
responses.response: I think this is the strongest argument against my position and I have moved toward it: it separates the platform from the mechanism, and I no longer treat the open pairing question as disqualifying. My remaining difficulty with B028 is different. It is the three-name limit, which forces the committee to leave out Cao and the first-author team and the Dean and Young groups, and the supply of names is a real problem for a field that is still moving quickly. By comparison the B022 credit is traceable and stable. I therefore keep B028 as my first alternative and not as my preferred prize, and I would accept it without strong objection if the committee turned to it.

responses.point: He prefers a two-part prize of B002 and B022, and agrees that the redefinition of the second should not be used to argue timing.
responses.response: I accept his correction and have removed the redefinition from my timing argument. On pairing, I still cannot support B002 with Halzen alone. Neither of us has stated a principle that makes one name the decisive credit for a collaboration of hundreds with an AMANDA predecessor, and the chair's own question 3 asks for one. Source identification is also less secure than the diffuse flux. I would add that B022 does not need a partner: a single clean achievement with two names is a complete prize, and pairing it with an unrelated part would dilute the citation and risk a second contested attribution.

responses.point: He moved from B003 to B028 and keeps B022 as an alternative, partly on the view that the clock is more technological than conceptual.
responses.response: I take the technological objection seriously. My answer is that the prizes have honoured instrument inventions when the instrument created a new measurement regime, and the magic-wavelength condition is a conceptual idea in atomic physics, not engineering: it is a statement about how to make a trapped ensemble behave like an isolated atom. I am glad you would not oppose B022 and accept your point that I should not claim more than the evidence supports about novelty relative to B028.

responses.point: She prefers B022 alone and wants the citation to state that it is distinct from comb-based and ion-clock work, and she doubts that B002 or B004 reach the attribution clarity of B022.
responses.response: I agree with her on both points. I have drafted the citation to name the lattice clock explicitly. I also accept her correction that the argument from record accuracy alone is weak, and I have rebuilt the case on what the capability makes possible and has already demonstrated. On B004 I share her concern about excluding Schmiedmayer and Chu, and I keep it only as a second alternative.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will judge the lattice clock distinct enough from the 2005 and 2012 prizes, which I think is the largest risk for B022.
Whether Katori and Ye adequately capture the credit, given Lemonde, the ion-clock groups and the second generation of lattice-clock experimenters.
Whether the B028 interpretation stabilises enough that its breadth of support should override my preference for a cleaner attribution.
How much of the fundamental-physics reach of the clocks is demonstrated and how much is still prospective.
statement.conflict_note: Disclosure as before: my profile documents a research stay in John Hall's laboratory in Boulder during my doctoral period, and Hall's JILA environment is part of the community from which the Ye group's precision-frequency work grew. I have no documented collaboration with Katori or Ye, and the chair has asked whether this requires recusal. I regard it as a disclosure for the record and leave it to the committee to decide; I will abstain if the committee considers recusal necessary. I also have documented connections to Svanberg, Aldén, Lund colleagues, WACQT and Deep Light Vision, none of which relate to B022.
